prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye, and round 1 has strengthened rather than weakened my reason. The discovery content, as I now put it, is that a many-atom optical lattice can be made compatible with a clock transition at the 10^-18 level: the magic wavelength is a statement about atomic structure, not about better engineering, as Lindroth argued. It was then verified by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), which is the replication I want before asking who deserves credit. What it lets us see is concrete: gravitational redshift across about a millimetre, with quantum mechanics and general relativity in the same laboratory, plus bounds on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter. No colleague has raised a scientific objection to the results themselves, and the two-name credit fits the three-person limit with room to spare. I would send the citation to the committee as worded above, naming magic-wavelength trapping and the lattice clock explicitly. That wording answers the chair's drafting question: it does not repeat the 2005 comb prize, which honoured the ruler that reads out an optical frequency, and it does not pre-empt a later nuclear-clock award to the thorium work, since it names a different oscillator.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is Olsson's, and I cannot dismiss it: the statutes reward the original discoverer, and Ye's strongest contribution may be taking Katori's invention to record accuracy, with much of the JILA accuracy work done by Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others. If the record shows Ye only improved a technique, the right configuration is Katori alone or a differently composed pair, and I should be willing to say so. A second reservation is that no variation of constants or dark-matter signal has appeared, so the physical reach is still prospective and the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes will lead some to read this as metrology. Finally, I moved here from my own opening first choice, the Higgs. I must not pretend that a problem of attribution has made the physics less important, and I do not want to be seen as using the clock as a comfortable place to hide.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye's contribution is original and decisive in its own right or an improvement of Katori's invention, and wants the record to separate Ye's results from those of Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others.
responses.response: I think the question is fair and I would rather answer it than wave it away. Katori has the priority on the proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstration. My case for Ye is that he brought the JILA strontium lattice clock, with a stable laser and comb-referenced readout, to uncertainties and coherence times that showed the magic-wavelength scheme works at the 10^-18 level, and later to many-body and Fermi-degenerate operation, which is not a repeat of Katori's experiment but a new regime of it. Group-leading credit for work done with students and postdocs is how the prize has usually worked, and Ludlow and Hinkley do not make the idea any less Ye's programme. I cannot verify the individual contributions from memory, so I would ask the AMO members to confirm that the specific JILA strontium results belong to Ye as originator. If they cannot, I would sooner go to Katori alone than weaken the credit, and I record that as my fallback.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, argues that the open pairing mechanism does not weaken the discovery claim, and accepts that B052 is the safest configuration while resting his preference on discovery type, not on maturity.
responses.response: I appreciate that Bernhard stated his preference by discovery type and not by maturity, because that is the real disagreement between us. I agree that an open pairing mechanism does not make the existence of the correlated phases a weak result, and as a theorist who distrusts unconfirmed elegance I like a model that told the experimenters where to look. My difficulty is the one Bernhard calls the weakest point of his own ballot: the three-name cut leaves out Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory, and two of three places go to a single theory paper. A prize that leaves an obvious claimant outside has to be justified by a very clear verdict on the science, and the attribution rule that would make me prefer B024 is a settled answer on Cao and the earlier theory. Until the committee has that, I rank B052 first and B024 as a field to revisit.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that lattice clocks are a discovery because the magic wavelength is a result about atomic structure, that the comb overlap should be handled by wording the citation around the lattice clock, and that a lattice-clock prize does not pre-empt a later nuclear-clock prize.
responses.response: I agree and I have adopted this framing in my citation. I would add a point she may find useful: a prize to Ye for the lattice clock does not sit comfortably as a prize for the whole of precision spectroscopy, so the committee should record explicitly that the thorium nuclear clock is outside this citation. I would not go as far as saying that the physics is already fully shown, since the consequences for constants and dark matter are still limits and not detections, and I would keep the citation on the established result, accuracy at the 10^-18 level, with the millimetre redshift measurement as the clue from nature. I also agree with her on B035: atom interferometry is a natural companion but with Chu missing from the set it is not a second part I can support this year.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube first to B052, said that atomic physics is outside his expertise, and asked that the AMO members test the case, with IceCube remaining his alternative.
responses.response: I welcome the chair's candour and I think it is right that the AMO members, and not the particle and astroparticle physicists, carry the lattice-clock priority record. Speaking as someone outside AMO as well, what persuades me is that the claim does not depend on one laboratory: the agreement at about 10^-18 across several national institutes is the kind of verification I can judge without being an expert. I also still regard IceCube as the best astroparticle candidate and a strong prize in a few years, once the source associations strengthen and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers are dealt with in the wording. I do not agree that it should be made a second part this year, because that would add a person and a contested credit for a result that is still early at the source level.

uncertainties: Whether the record shows Ye's own contribution to the lattice clock as original and decisive; if not, a Katori-only credit would be the more defensible configuration.
Whether the committee will read lattice clocks as a discovery or as instrumentation, given the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes, and whether the proposed citation wording is enough.
I am still recalling lattice-clock priority details (Katori versus Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto and the Yb, Hg and Al+ groups) from memory and have not verified them.
Whether a fair three-name or organisational formulation of the ATLAS and CMS Higgs observation exists; I do not see one, and it stays an alternative only.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for the preferred configuration: my ties are to my PhD supervisor David Gross, the late Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string-theory group, none related to Katori, Ye or B052. I stay without conflict on B043 and B010. B041 (Event Horizon Telescope) lies close to my own horizonless black-hole mimicker work and I would raise that and step back if it came to a vote, but it is in nobody's configuration.
